headline: Google expands Gemini Spark access to more AI Pro and Ultra users globally
summary: The agentic AI assistant, powered by Gemini 3.5, is now available to all Google AI Pro users in the US and Ultra users worldwide, excluding some regions. Free users are still not included.
details: Google is expanding access to its Gemini Spark agentic AI assistant, making it available to more paid subscribers. All Google AI Pro users in the US ($20/month) and Google AI Ultra users globally ($100-$200/month) can now access Spark, though free users are still excluded. Note that users in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, the UK, and Nigeria are not included in this global rollout.

Spark, powered by Gemini 3.5, is deeply integrated into Google's Workspace apps, enabling advanced task automation. Users can assign tasks by accessing Spark via the sidebar on a computer or through the menu on mobile devices.

This AI assistant can check emails and calendar schedules, prioritize tasks, draft email responses, and summarize lengthy threads. It can also create detailed reports in Google Docs from meeting notes and emails, offering a wide range of productivity enhancements.

headline: The Subprime Datacenter Crisis draws parallels to 2008 mortgage market collapse
summary: An analysis by Zitron compares the current AI bubble and datacenter investments to the speculative financial practices that led to the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, warning of systemic weakness.
details: The article draws a stark parallel between the current "AI bubble" and the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, suggesting a potential "Subprime Datacenter Crisis." It highlights how speculation and hype can create systemic weaknesses in financial markets.

The comparison references "The Big Short," where synthetic collateralized debt obligations (CDOs) allowed multiple parties to bet on the same underlying mortgages. This created a market 20 times larger than the actual mortgage bond market.

Thousands of mortgage bonds were referenced in CDOs tens of thousands of times, meaning a single default could trigger widespread financial carnage. Bonds were routinely misrated by agencies, obscuring the true risk.

Warnings about the system's instability, like those from IMF Chief Economist Raghuram Rajan in 2005, were dismissed by figures like Larry Summers. Meanwhile, institutions like Lehman Brothers were lauded for their "conservative" credit derivatives practices just years before their collapse.

This speculative environment was fueled by a "global savings glut" in the early 2000s, pushing down yields and forcing investors into riskier assets. Low interest rates post-dot-com bubble further incentivized financial institutions to create complex, dangerous CDOs.
